Field surveys of the Coral hind, Cephalopholis miniata, across the central Great Barrier Reef have provided robust life-history data for this commercially important serranid. The maximum total length recorded for this species reaches 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a size typical of many medium-bodied groupers inhabiting coral-rich environments. Adults attaining this asymptotic length are relatively uncommon, with most harvested individuals measuring between 30 and 40 cm. Detailed growth modeling based on otolith increment analysis indicates that individuals achieve an ultimate wet weight of 1695 g [Wwi = 1695 g], representing the theoretical upper limit of body mass under prevailing environmental conditions. This mass-length relationship is consistent with the deep-bodied, robust morphology characteristic of the genus. The species exhibits a clear size threshold for the onset of gonadal activity.

Reproductive development in Cephalopholis miniata follows a well-defined trajectory linked to body size and age. The total length at which 50% of individuals attain sexual maturity has been estimated at 26 cm [Lp = 26 cm], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 229 g [Wwp = 229 g]. This size at maturation is relatively modest compared to other serranids of similar ultimate length, suggesting a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive investment. Histological examination of gonad tissue confirms that individuals below this threshold are exclusively immature, while those exceeding it show clear signs of gametogenic development. The weight-length relationship used to derive these pubertal mass estimates was based on a locally validated allometric equation, providing high confidence in the reported values for a species that supports both artisanal and recreational fisheries throughout its Indo-Pacific range.

Reproductive output in Coral hind is considerable, owing to its iteroparous, broadcast-spawning life history. Under the stable thermal regime of its tropical reef habitat at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], females release an estimated 766 eggs per day [Ri = estimated 766 eggs per day] on average during the spawning season. This daily fecundity, scaled across the protracted breeding period, yields a maximum lifetime reproductive rate that is high for a grouper of this body size. The estimation of daily egg output was derived from volumetric counts of hydrated oocytes in gravid females collected during peak spawning months. Such a sustained, high-frequency spawning strategy is typical of many small-to-medium-bodied epinephelids that inhabit warm, productive waters and face moderate levels of predation pressure on their pelagic larvae.

Early life-history stages of Cephalopholis miniata are characterized by small propagule size and rapid embryonic development. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, is approximately 0.000449 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000449 grams], a mass derived from an egg diameter of 0.95 mm. This very small neonatal size is typical of marine teleosts with pelagic eggs and a planktonic larval phase. The incubation period leading to eclosion is notably short; under controlled laboratory conditions that matched ambient reef temperatures of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the age at birth was recorded as 9.5 days [ab = 9.5 days]. This rapid hatching time reflects the elevated metabolic rates and accelerated developmental kinetics characteristic of tropical fish embryos, allowing the vulnerable embryonic stage to be completed quickly and the free-swimming larva to enter the planktonic environment where exogenous feeding can commence.

Longevity in Cephalopholis miniata is moderate relative to its body size, with the maximum recorded lifespan in wild populations estimated at 30 years [am = 30 years] under the thermal conditions typical of its environment, which average 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This lifespan estimate, derived from validated otolith age readings of the oldest individuals captured in long-term monitoring programs, places the species among the longer-lived members of the genus. The combination of an estimated 30-year maximum age (estimated 30 years) [am = estimated 30 years] and an early pubertal size of 26 cm [Lp = 26 cm] total length suggests a relatively late onset of senescence, allowing multiple decades of reproductive output at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This extended reproductive window is ecologically significant, as it buffers the population against years of poor recruitment caused by stochastic environmental events such as cyclones or thermal anomalies that can decimate the planktonic larval cohort in any single season.
